newsitem.title: USA: Miami residents scramble for Brink's loot.
newsitem.headline: Miami residents scramble for Brink's loot.

text.p: Some said it was like Christmas in January. Others called it pennies from heaven.

Residents of a poor Miami neighborhood scrambled on hands and knees Wednesday to grab a share of a fortune in cash that showered into the street from a security firm's armored car that crashed into a guardrail.

A police spokesman said "pandemonium" reigned in Overtown, just north of downtown Miami, when a Brink's truck overturned during rush hour on a highway overpass, cracked open and sent a river of bundled currency and coins onto a street below.
"There was money everywhere," Lt. Bill Schwartz said. "You couldn't walk anywhere without stepping on money. The streets were paved with gold."
Dozens of people, many on their knees, scooped up bills and coins, then scattered as police sirens were heard.
"They were sticking it in bags, boxes, anything. Sticking it in their pockets, pants and shirts. Fighting each other for the money," Schwartz said.
Firefighters and police used shovels to scoop up cash from the street. Schwartz said one firefighter had found a bag containing about $300,000.
Some residents told reporters they considered the cash "pennies from heaven" -- a late Christmas present to a needy neighborhood.
"These hardworking people, they don't make enough money. God sent it to them," one man said.

Schwartz said he had heard talk on the street that the truck carried as much as $3 million and up to $500,000 might be missing, but Brink's had refused to tell police how much the truck carried or how much it had lost.
A Brink's spokesman said the company would not comment on the incident.
Police said anyone who picked up money could be charged with theft, but conceded it would be difficult to track the missing cash and those who took it. No one had been charged.
"This is theft," Schwartz said. "If you pick up one quarter that came from that truck up there, that is theft."
After police left the scene, residents returned to pick up stray coins from the dirt.
